paragraph "Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (née Byron; 10 December 1815 – 27 November 1852), also known as Ada Lovelace, was an English mathematician and writer chiefly known for work on Charles Babbage's"
[ax-14448467455531664878] link "née"
[ax-2533844263545388030] link "mathematician"
[ax-15610648908925387361] link "writer"
[ax-8994056290354502447] link "Charles Babbage"
[ax-3538390797048712810] link "computer"
[ax-10119420612326056583] link "analytical engine"
[ax-8722019988520602847] link "computer programmer"
paragraph "Lovelace was the only legitimate child of poet Lord Byron and reformer Anne Isabella Milbanke.[2] Lord Byron separated from his wife a month after Ada was born, and died when she was eight. Although o"
[ax-7192126967244850626] link "legitimate child"
[ax-1395677742473341422] link "Lord Byron"
[ax-13759705934390316641] link "Anne Isabella Milbanke"
[ax-7156393845131516133] link "[2]"
[ax-2453725563799549915] link "assiduously"
[ax-10006489486430478530] link "William King"
[ax-11847641830464767832] link "Baron"
[ax-9326442917301746257] link "Earl of Lovelace"
[ax-12941163665601312428] link "Baron Lovelaces"
[ax-6059874633401622977] link "[3]"
paragraph "Lovelace's educational and social exploits brought her into contact with scientists such as Andrew Crosse, Charles Babbage, David Brewster, Charles Wheatstone and Michael Faraday, and the author Charl"
[ax-9554634162210317224] link "Andrew Crosse"
[ax-8482169570950777006] link "David Brewster"
[ax-4933418183498987067] link "Charles Wheatstone"
[ax-772705880368084178] link "Michael Faraday"
[ax-9990076571906235238] link "Charles Dickens"
[ax-8318545879034129798] link "[4]"
[ax-12363021373029810962] link "Metaphysician"
[ax-2115826809143201823] link "[5]"
paragraph "At age 18, Lovelace's mathematical talents led her to a long working relationship and friendship with fellow British mathematician Charles Babbage. She was particularly interested in Babbage's work on"
[ax-15450209724536058982] link "Charles Babbage's Saturday night soirées"
[ax-5877796542271985400] link "[6]"
[ax-1720568966596481990] link "Mary Somerville"
[ax-3356711918732227401] link "Turing-complete"
[ax-5327251752960530892] link "an article"
[ax-4904019140574307898] link "Luigi Menabrea"
[ax-5307745002192205069] link "seven long explanatory notes"
[ax-6211180199944171652] link "Bernoulli numbers"
[ax-6989597840408312197] link "computer program"
paragraph "She developed a vision of the capability of computers to go beyond mere calculating or number-crunching, while many others, including Babbage, focused only on those capabilities.[7] Lovelace was the f"
[ax-9177782137422149276] link "calculating"
[ax-4379377958447261243] link "[7]"
[ax-11140777010185470614] link "arithmetical"

paragraph "On 21 April, Lord Byron signed the deed of separation, although very reluctantly, and left England for good a few days later.[13] Aside from an acrimonious separation, Lady Byron continued throughout "
[ax-5362905956235992595] link "deed of separation"
[ax-3414882904190948509] link "[13]"
[ax-13027003343739121786] link "[14]"
[ax-9849136332212848952] link "[15]"

paragraph "Lovelace did not have a close relationship with her mother. She was often left in the care of her maternal grandmother Judith, Hon. Lady Milbanke, who doted on her. However, because of societal attitu"
[ax-8546802770149869964] link "[17]"
[ax-2738185485254532853] link "[18]"

[ax-2253131431601345915] link "measles"

paragraph "Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (née Byron; 10 December 1815 – 27 November 1852), also known as Ada Lovelace, was an English mathematician and writer chiefly known for work on Charles Babbage's"
[ax-14448467455531664878] link "née"
[ax-2533844263545388030] link "mathematician"
[ax-15610648908925387361] link "writer"
[ax-8994056290354502447] link "Charles Babbage"
[ax-3538390797048712810] link "computer"
[ax-10119420612326056583] link "analytical engine"
[ax-8722019988520602847] link "computer programmer"
paragraph "Lovelace was the only legitimate child of poet Lord Byron and reformer Anne Isabella Milbanke.[2] Lord Byron separated from his wife a month after Ada was born, and died when she was eight. Although o"
[ax-7192126967244850626] link "legitimate child"
[ax-1395677742473341422] link "Lord Byron"
[ax-13759705934390316641] link "Anne Isabella Milbanke"
[ax-7156393845131516133] link "[2]"
[ax-2453725563799549915] link "assiduously"
[ax-10006489486430478530] link "William King"
[ax-11847641830464767832] link "Baron"
[ax-9326442917301746257] link "Earl of Lovelace"
[ax-12941163665601312428] link "Baron Lovelaces"
[ax-6059874633401622977] link "[3]"
paragraph "Lovelace's educational and social exploits brought her into contact with scientists such as Andrew Crosse, Charles Babbage, David Brewster, Charles Wheatstone and Michael Faraday, and the author Charl"
[ax-9554634162210317224] link "Andrew Crosse"
[ax-8482169570950777006] link "David Brewster"
[ax-4933418183498987067] link "Charles Wheatstone"
[ax-772705880368084178] link "Michael Faraday"
[ax-9990076571906235238] link "Charles Dickens"
[ax-8318545879034129798] link "[4]"
[ax-12363021373029810962] link "Metaphysician"
[ax-2115826809143201823] link "[5]"
paragraph "At age 18, Lovelace's mathematical talents led her to a long working relationship and friendship with fellow British mathematician Charles Babbage. She was particularly interested in Babbage's work on"
[ax-15450209724536058982] link "Charles Babbage's Saturday night soirées"
[ax-5877796542271985400] link "[6]"
[ax-1720568966596481990] link "Mary Somerville"
[ax-3356711918732227401] link "Turing-complete"
[ax-5327251752960530892] link "an article"
[ax-4904019140574307898] link "Luigi Menabrea"
[ax-5307745002192205069] link "seven long explanatory notes"
[ax-6211180199944171652] link "Bernoulli numbers"
[ax-6989597840408312197] link "computer program"
paragraph "She developed a vision of the capability of computers to go beyond mere calculating or number-crunching, while many others, including Babbage, focused only on those capabilities.[7] Lovelace was the f"
[ax-9177782137422149276] link "calculating"
[ax-4379377958447261243] link "[7]"
[ax-11140777010185470614] link "arithmetical"
[ax-11936516662498271542] link "music"
[ax-10974197721990276199] link "[8]"
[ax-9570128646909217366] link "programming language"

paragraph "Lord Byron expected his child to be a \"glorious boy\" and was disappointed when Lady Byron gave birth to a girl.[9] The child was named after Byron's half-sister, Augusta Leigh, and was called \"Ada\" by"

[ax-16384665990182109343] link "Lady Byron"

paragraph "On 21 April, Lord Byron signed the deed of separation, although very reluctantly, and left England for good a few days later.[13] Aside from an acrimonious separation, Lady Byron continued throughout "
[ax-5362905956235992595] link "deed of separation"
[ax-3414882904190948509] link "[13]"
[ax-13027003343739121786] link "[14]"
[ax-9849136332212848952] link "[15]"

[ax-2648509337282510951] link "Somerville College, Oxford"
paragraph "Lovelace did not have a close relationship with her mother. She was often left in the care of her maternal grandmother Judith, Hon. Lady Milbanke, who doted on her. However, because of societal attitu"
[ax-8546802770149869964] link "[17]"
[ax-2738185485254532853] link "[18]"
[ax-8478823427782833052] link "[19]"
[ax-199049148008873724] link ""

paragraph "Lovelace was often ill, beginning in early childhood. At the age of eight, she experienced headaches that obscured her vision.[10] In June 1829, she was paralyzed after a bout of measles. She was subj"
[ax-12251210119207197227] link "[10]"
[ax-2253131431601345915] link "measles"
blockquote "When Ada was twelve years old, this future \"Lady Fairy\", as Charles Babbage affectionately called her, decided she wanted to fly. Ada Byron went about the project methodically, thoughtfully, with imag"
paragraph "When Ada was twelve years old, this future \"Lady Fairy\", as Charles Babbage affectionately called her, decided she wanted to fly. Ada Byron went about the project methodically, thoughtfully, with imag"

[ax-15722590763232250327] link "[8]"
paragraph "Ada Byron had an affair with a tutor in early 1833. She tried to elope with him after she was caught, but the tutor's relatives recognised her and contacted her mother. Lady Byron and her friends cove"
[ax-17258492572332265104] link "[20]"
[ax-6281448185685965909] link "Allegra"

paragraph "On 8 July 1835, she married William, 8th Baron King, becoming Lady King. They had three homes: Ockham Park, Surrey; a Scottish estate on Loch Torridon in Ross-shire; and a house in London. They spent "
[ax-18282496243978291679] link "William, 8th Baron King"
[ax-6334597464471510353] link "Ockham Park"
[ax-15019737515387827658] link "Loch Torridon"

[ax-794528221925498897] link "Tudorbethan"
[ax-6130292409834093769] link "Charles Barry"
[ax-12869925551132394333] link "[26]"
[ax-6464757734172314499] link "[27]"
paragraph "They had three children: Byron (born 1836); Anne Isabella (called Annabella, born 1837); and Ralph Gordon (born 1839). Immediately after the birth of Annabella, Lady King experienced \"a tedious and su"
[ax-8499816004773310408] link "Byron"
[ax-8328949065407043719] link "Anne Isabella"
[ax-5509584985651322605] link "Ralph Gordon"
[ax-2111964893444820358] link "[25]"
[ax-10291301559874829009] link "Barons Lovelace"

[ax-14234432576164500041] link "[28]"
[ax-16774040659907589791] link "William Benjamin Carpenter"
[ax-3107027452540432530] link "[29]"
[ax-16583865629265321750] link "[30]"
paragraph "In 1841, Lovelace and Medora Leigh (the daughter of Lord Byron's half-sister Augusta Leigh) were told by Ada's mother that Ada's father was also Medora's father.[31] On 27 February 1841, Ada wrote to "
[ax-15950908314380740062] link "Medora Leigh"
[ax-14940716804391217746] link "[31]"
[ax-3805212175218299329] link "[32]"
[ax-13557303819331144863] link "[33]"

paragraph "From 1832, when she was seventeen, her mathematical abilities began to emerge,[23] and her interest in mathematics dominated the majority of her adult life.[39] Her mother's obsession with rooting out"
[ax-16524814617860960261] link "[23]"
[ax-9402661690669397688] link "[39]"
[ax-12801194183007920023] link "William Frend"
[ax-1647018122400352874] link "William King"
[ax-18155485914800073979] link "[a]"
[ax-3093020686459668147] link "Mary Somerville"
[ax-5761997506952309763] link "Augustus De Morgan"
[ax-2147653585722544159] link "numbers of Bernoulli"
[ax-4173296462279545608] link "[40]"
[ax-4504616476465287167] link "[41]"
paragraph "Lovelace often questioned basic assumptions through integrating poetry and science. Whilst studying differential calculus, she wrote to De Morgan:"
[ax-9710370700750436728] link "differential calculus"
blockquote "I may remark that the curious transformations many formulae can undergo, the unsuspected and to a beginner apparently impossible identity of forms exceedingly dissimilar at first sight, is I think one"
paragraph "I may remark that the curious transformations many formulae can undergo, the unsuspected and to a beginner apparently impossible identity of forms exceedingly dissimilar at first sight, is I think one"
[ax-4720837125105413136] link "[42]"
paragraph "Lovelace believed that intuition and imagination were critical to effectively applying mathematical and scientific concepts. She valued metaphysics as much as mathematics, viewing both as tools for ex"
[ax-903387595825114067] link "metaphysics"
[ax-7524436214858525781] link "[43]"

[ax-6668362006780918681] link ""
text "Painting of Lovelace seated at a piano, by (1852). Although in great pain at the time, she agreed to sit for the painting as her father, , had been painted by Phillips' father, ."

paragraph "Lovelace died at the age of 36 on 27 November 1852[44] from cervical cancer (which contemporary accounts called uterine cancer, since a distinction between the two was not made at that time).[45][46] "
[ax-4860171959588656847] link "[44]"
[ax-4231723535803722369] link "cervical cancer"

paragraph "Throughout her life, Lovelace was strongly interested in scientific developments and fads of the day, including phrenology[50] and mesmerism.[51] After her work with Babbage, Lovelace continued to wor"
[ax-9478231873205784300] link "phrenology"
[ax-10512332414207462014] link "[50]"
[ax-17662243292408240149] link "mesmerism"

[ax-1153688560472058797] link "[55]"

paragraph "Lovelace first met Charles Babbage in June 1833, through their mutual friend Mary Somerville. Later that month, Babbage invited Lovelace to see the prototype for his difference engine.[56] She became "
[ax-454260153583655645] link "Charles Babbage"
[ax-13746769770128352999] link "difference engine"
[ax-2668150744723660069] link "[56]"
[ax-3102609194966257456] link "[57]"
[ax-15509982013555336034] link "[b]"
blockquote "Forget this world and all its troubles and if possible its multitudinous Charlatans—every thing in short but the Enchantress of Number.[57]"
paragraph "Forget this world and all its troubles and if possible its multitudinous Charlatans—every thing in short but the Enchantress of Number.[57]"
[ax-5959409972451675305] link "[57]"

[ax-1483906291053091306] link "[58]"
heading "Babbage's lecture, Menabrea's French transcription, Lovelace's translation and Notes A-G"
paragraph "In 1840, Babbage was invited to give a seminar at the University of Turin about his Analytical Engine. Luigi Menabrea, a young Italian engineer and the future Prime Minister of Italy, transcribed Babb"
[ax-10761876033652904883] link "University of Turin"
[ax-7080232749622363777] link "Luigi Menabrea"
[ax-1792241703698628621] link "Prime Minister of Italy"
[ax-14538691499110972218] link "Bibliothèque universelle de Genève"
[ax-639484121981252344] link "Charles Wheatstone"
paragraph "During a nine-month period in 1842–43, Lovelace translated Menabrea's article.[59] She augmented the paper with seven notes, A to G, about three times longer than the translation.[60] The translation "
[ax-6833872749582784460] link "[59]"
[ax-16799080081966601083] link "[60]"
[ax-15475472126590686177] link "Scientific Memoirs"
[ax-4857960289620510876] link "[61]"
paragraph "Explaining the Analytical Engine's function was a difficult task; many other scientists did not grasp the concept and the British establishment had shown little interest in it.[62] Lovelace's notes ev"
[ax-16700968202956411956] link "[62]"
[ax-11950568452310605037] link "[63]"
[ax-18443247017606365528] link "Michael Faraday"
[ax-11170642272044702550] link "[64]"
heading "Babbage's preface"
paragraph "Lovelace and Babbage had a minor falling out when the papers were published, when he tried to leave his own statement (criticising the government's treatment of his Engine) as an unsigned preface, whi"
[ax-3217228174514669428] link "Taylor"
[ax-14033456340947946475] link "Scientific Memoirs"
[ax-3353481785614122320] link "Benjamin Woolley"
[ax-9476644773365900344] link "[65]"
[ax-16745465130136723447] link "[64]"

paragraph "The notes are important in the early history of computers, especially since Note G[66] described, in complete detail, a method for calculating a sequence of Bernoulli numbers using the Analytical Engi"
[ax-4250653863875278911] link "history of computers"
[ax-17709600139577384628] link "Note G"

[ax-594633608243216132] link "[70]"
[ax-7562445253499278965] link "algorithm"
[ax-6584286208888131254] link "[71]"
paragraph "In 1953, more than a century after her death, Ada Lovelace's notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine were republished as an appendix to B. V. Bowden's Faster than Thought: A Symposium on Digital Computin"
[ax-5424535690373859113] link "B. V. Bowden"
[ax-4168500996075967612] link "[72]"
[ax-8236053079889542886] link "[67]"
heading "Controversy over contribution"
paragraph "Based on this work, Lovelace is often called the first computer programmer[73][74] and her method has been called the world's first computer program.[75][76][77]"
[ax-12939936192771356765] link "[73]"
[ax-5808433314017186825] link "[74]"
[ax-10220031696683665491] link "[75]"
[ax-5280727109328798808] link "[76]"
[ax-13244506002188974044] link "[77]"
paragraph "Eugene Eric Kim and Lovelace biographer, Betty Alexandra Toole, argued it was \"incorrect\" to regard Lovelace as the first computer programmer in an article for Scientific American.[71] Babbage claims "
[ax-15252778699756847026] link "Scientific American"
